metadata.title: Evaluación de un juego serio que contribuye a fortalecer el razonamiento lógico-matemático en estudiantes de nivel medio superior
metadata.venue: RIED. Revista Iberoamericana de Educación a Distancia

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study evaluates a serious game intervention with a small, single-institution sample of 33 high-school students in Mexico, using pre- and post-tests and game-usage logs. The methodology describes recording response times and correctness for two custom multiple-choice exams and analyzing differences with Welch’s t-test, but it does not report the use of any complex survey design or sampling weights. Because the analysis is based on a convenience classroom/school sample rather than an ILSA-style representative design, no ILSA weight variables (e.g., W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT) are specified. The only explicit data cleaning step is outlier removal for response-time lists using Grubbs’ test; no PV scaling or IRT/WLE procedures are involved.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variables are not ILSA cognitive achievement scores with Plausible Values; instead, the study uses custom multiple-choice exam scores (correct/incorrect) and performance levels derived from the game’s fuzzy-logic rules (e.g., advance/regress) plus response times. Because the paper does not describe any missing-data protocol for student responses or log entries, missing-data handling is not reported. This is a reporting gap for transparency, although the small sample and the described exclusion/outlier steps suggest the authors may have relied on available complete records for the pre/post comparisons.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Participants were 33 students from the last semester (sixth semester) of the Escuela Industrial y Preparatoria Técnica Álvaro Obregón Unidad Tres Caminos, Universidad Autónoma de Nuevo León (Mexico). All participants were high-school (nivel medio superior) students enrolled in mathematics courses (arithmetic, algebra, statistics) and were administered a first exam, then used the serious game for two weeks, and then took a second exam. The paper also reports a separate larger dataset (307 students) used to calibrate/validate the fuzzy inference system timing rules from game problem responses, but the learning evaluation sample for the pre/post comparison is 33. For the timing rules, outliers were removed from the correct/incorrect response-time lists using Grubbs’ test (R), and reported-time bounds were used to define the fuzzy sets (corto/medio/largo).

main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using ILSA assessment context not specified in extraction (heuristic migration) the study leveraged the reported predictors to predict Primary study outcome (heuristic migration), finding that This paper evaluates a serious game (“MathLogic - La Leyenda de YuZhen”) designed to strengthen logical-mathematical reasoning in Mexican upper-secondary students. The study uses a pre/post design: students took a first multiple-choice exam, then used the game for two weeks, and finally took a second exam; performance was analyzed using response time and correctness, and game progression (advance/regress) was determined by a fuzzy inference system based on time and correctness. The reported results show that students who used the game (and/or advanced levels) improved more than those who did not: average exam performance increased from 52 to 58 for game users versus 66 to 60 for non-users (time=0 group). The paper also reports that students who advanced at least to the next level (level 2) showed improvement in the second evaluation, with Welch hypothesis tests reported at 95% probability. Limitations include the absence of ML model training/validation, no survey-weighting framework, and limited transparency on missing-data handling. This indicates that these patterns have implications for educational policy and instructional practice, though cross-sectional ILSA designs cannot establish causality.

data.null_fields_interpretation: The extraction is sparse for ML-specific fields because the study does not train or compare machine-learning predictive models on ILSA microdata. Instead, it implements a fuzzy-logic system inside a serious game and uses Welch’s t-tests to compare pre/post exam outcomes and progression indicators. Therefore, plausible-values handling, missing-data handling, and ML technique fields are not applicable or not reported in the ML sense, and main_findings are left empty because the paper does not provide ML target-variable prediction metrics (e.g., accuracy/AUC/RMSE) from a supervised learning model.
